newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Airline disasters force world aviation industry to act.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Airline disasters force world aviation industry to act.

text.p: It has never been safer to travel by air, but screaming headlines and charred bodies seem to tell quite another story.

Fearing a collapse in consumer confidence after a string of high-profile air disasters this year, the aviation industry is redoubling its efforts to cut the accident rate and persuade the travelling public that they have nothing to fear.
On November 12, 349 people were killed when a Saudi Arabian Boeing 747 hit a Kazakh jet over India. Five days earlier, 151 died when a Nigerian Boeing 727 crashed on an internal flight.
The volume of air travel is set to double in the next 20 years and if the crash rate remains constant, one airliner will be destroyed every week by 2010.
"If you have more aircraft and the same degree of risk, there will be more accidents -- that's just maths," said David Learmount, air safety editor at Flight International magazine.
Learmount, who compiles an annual list of the world's air disasters, said although around 1,900 people had died so far this year, 1996 was likely to be an unfortunate aberration.
"Around 1,000 passengers a year die on average. Given that 1.5 billion people travel a year by air, it's not that desperate.
"It will be much safer after this year. In order for the overall trend to continue, next year there will have to be a lower than average number of accidents," he said.

But this is of little consolation to an increasingly worried industry. The International Air Transport Association (IATA), which groups the world's airlines, says it wants the accident rate to be halved in the next decade.
"We cannot afford to have one accident a week, even with the doubling of traffic. It would be devastating for the industry," said IATA public relations chief William Gaillard.
"It would never be off the front pages of the newspapers. People would begin to seriously question the industry," he said by telephone from Geneva.
"Car accidents don't get into the newspapers, but every tiny air crash in every tiny country is heard around the world."

Airliners are now safer than ever before but manufacturers cannot afford to be complacent, since blaming pilots, ground crews or air traffic controllers is of little solace if the public decides a particular make of aircraft is unsafe.
"There are significant commercial risks. It's a competitive world and people can choose who they fly with and what planes they fly on," said an official at one major manufacturer.

Recent disasters have raised urgent questions about the risks posed by terrorism, ageing airliners and patchy air traffic control in developing countries -- but these factors rarely cause catastrophes.
Instead, the multi-billion dollar industry is focusing its efforts on the pilots.

More than 75 percent of all air accidents are caused by human error and evidence is increasing that aircrew are less capable of handling the high technology installed in the cockpit in a bid to make their lives easier.

"Anyone can fly one of these modern planes when the conditions are normal. But when the pressure is on, it depends on the individual. Technology does overwhelm some people to a degree," said Chris Partridge, an analyst at aviation consultants Avmark.
"Many crashes are caused by pilots not knowing where they are and not understanding what instruments are telling them."
A China Airlines Airbus crashed in Japan in 1994, killing 264 people, after the flight crew fought with the autopilot as they tried to land the plane.
A British Midland Boeing 737 crash-landed in 1989 when an engine caught fire, killing 47 people, after the crew somehow misread the instruments and shut down the wrong power plant.
And although ground proximity warning systems are becoming ever more sophisticated, pilots still crash into high terrain with depressing frequency.
"This happens the whole time. You can invest all you want and it comes down to human error," said Partridge.
In private, aircraft makers are tearing out their hair in frustration as they see their airliners involved in one avoidable catastrophe after another.
The official investigation report into the February 1996 crash of a Turkish-owned Boeing B-757 off the Dominican Republic, which killed 189 people, pulled no punches.
The plane dived into the sea because pilots ignored the stick-shaker, a basic instrument which vibrates the joystick to warn of an impending stall.

The report blamed the crash on the pilots' failure to cope with instrument failure, their lack of basic flying skills and poor knowledge of flight procedures. But it did not blame the crew, saying they had met the internationally-accepted requirements for pilots.
Instead, the report reserved its fire for the airlines and manufacturers, saying training had not kept up to pace with the modernisation of aircraft.
It spurred the industry to look again at how it trained its pilots, especially at the tricky question of how to tackle human error.
"We've now reached a watershed by accepting that human error is normal," said Dr Michael Bagshaw, head of aviation medical services at British Airways.
"The old approach was to think that human error was a mistake which should be avoided. Now we have to assume it will happen and instead assess how pilots cope with error."

Experts say these errors are more likely to occur in developing countries where the infrastructure has not managed to keep pace with booming air traffic and maintenance of aircraft can sometimes be haphazard.

"The real problem is with developing economies -- 12 percent of operators have 80 percent of the accidents. Where are the accidents happening? The Dominican Republic, Peru, Africa, the former Soviet Union," said Learmount.

Airline pilots complain about substandard air traffic control systems in many parts of the world but U.S. officials say the gradual shift from ground-based to space-based air traffic control will increase safety.

U.S. authorities are also trying to persuade airlines to swap data so an incident discovered by one carrier on its plane does not become a system-wide design flaw which could make that type accident prone.
But there is still no cure for human error.

Last week U.S. safety officials recommended airlines find ways to ensure that flight indicator vents were not accidently taped shut, thought to have been a cause of the October crash of an AeroPeru Boeing 757 which killed 70 people.

And British Airways said recently that a missile had exploded some 10,000 feet (3,000 metres) below one of its airliners flying over Turkey after staff failed to feed details of a planned military exercise into a computer.
